translations.text: Hippolytus's interpretation of the blessings of Moses to the twelve tribes. Kyrie eleison!
The blessings that the blessed Isaac gave to his sons have been set forth in the earlier books, and the meaning of the things that took place has not been passed over in silence.
And those of Jacob too, which were recorded concerning the twelve sons and were explained in the same manner,
namely, what the blessings were that were given and upon whom they were fulfilled, and what the prophecies are and upon whom they were fulfilled.
Now, by grace from the Lord, I will begin to set forth the blessings of Moses as well, how he blessed the twelve tribes, and I will omit nothing,
for he is altogether perfect, a man made firm and shown to be fully perfect upon the foundation of salvation,
having understood by faith the things spoken by the prophets and now fulfilled by Christ, and having been inseparable from his righteousness.
But it is better for us to recount the words of the faithful Moses, to make mention of his birth, and to set forth his deeds precisely, with nothing left out.
When he was one hundred and twenty years old, he gathered the people beyond the Jordan and blessed the twelve tribes, just as Jacob had told in his counsel,
that there is someone there, hidden among the tribes, the blessed Son begotten of the Father, not yet revealed in the flesh in the world.
This Moses was born in the land of the Egyptians, while the sons of Israel were sojourning there, of the tribe of Levi, of his father Amram and his mother Jochebed.
His brother was Aaron and his sister Miriam. He, cast out at three months old on the bank of the river, placed in an ark and taken out by the daughter of Pharaoh, was raised in the royal house.
And when he was forty years old, he resolved to visit his brothers, the sons of Israel. Seeing a Hebrew being overpowered, he came to his aid and struck down the Egyptian.
And Pharaoh heard of it and sought to kill him. But he became a fugitive and lived as a stranger in the land of the Midianites.
And he tended the sheep of Jethro, his father-in-law. And he was seventy years old.
And he led the people out of the land of the Egyptians by the command of God. He sent ten plagues upon Egypt.
He arrived in the desert. And he went up Mount Sinai and brought down the commandments from the living God, which were to guard his own people.
But those who had come out of Egypt were six hundred thousand.
And they did not obey God, and all of them were struck down in the desert. And in their place God raised up their sons,
whom Moses numbered and arranged, each of them by tribes, each according to their fathers, so that they might make up those six hundred thousand.
This was the occasion for Moses, in accordance with that command of God. He chose twelve men, rulers of their tribes,
and sent them to view the land. And ten of them came back and stirred up the people, and being terror-stricken they grew afraid and said
that the land is evil and the men cunning and man-eating, and the cities very great and walled,
and the men who dwell in it are men great in stature and [?]. And they spoke of them as of the offspring of giants.
And they made them appear before them as locusts. When the people heard this, they became terror-stricken in heart and were greatly afraid.
And they sat day and night and reproached Moses, wanting to turn back to Egypt.
Two of those who had surveyed that land, who were found faithful, stood up against them, tried to restrain them, and said:
"The land that we went through is very beautiful, a land that flows with honey and milk. Behold, this is its fruit."
They showed them its abundant fruit, and there was a cluster of grapes carried on a pole on their shoulders. But they did not believe, and they plotted to stone them.
And so, because of the unbelief and the rebellion that took place there, the Lord made a promise to Moses with an oath and said to him:
"These men who have embittered me and did not believe my words,
who saw signs and wonders in the land of Egypt, shall not see the good land that I promised to their fathers."
"But these children, of whom they said that they would become captives of the enemies, to these I will give that land, and to Joshua son of Nun,
and my servant Caleb son of Jephunneh, for the Spirit was upon him. I will bring them in there and give them that land which they surveyed with their feet,"
because of which that people were kept in the wilderness for forty years, and all of them perished according to the word of the Lord.
But those two men, of whom he had spoken beforehand, and their sons, having grown up, were joined to the number in place of their fathers, those whom he called.
The blessed Moses, beyond the Jordan, taught the second law to the fathers who were born from above and perfect.
That law was not another law given to them beyond the former one that he gave to their fathers, but he wrote the same one,
so that they might take heed concerning their fathers who had gone out from the land of Egypt, and so that in that wilderness they might fear the Lord with all their heart.
At that time Moses, by the Spirit, arranged the twelve tribes into two parts.
He gave the blessings on Mount Gerizim through the mouth of six of the tribes, and the curses on Mount Ebal through the mouth of the other six.
And it is not idly that he shows us this beforehand, for he divided the tribes into two parts,
showing that some of them, through Christ, by that blessing, would inherit with their own fathers in the new law, on the right,
being found there, and that others, held fast by the old error, because of their unbelief would be handed over under the curse, on the left.
As the Savior says to those who are like them: "At that time I will say to those who are at my right:
Come, you blessed of my Father, and inherit the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world.
And you who are on the left, depart from me, you cursed, into the eternal fire which my Father prepared for the devil and his servants."
Now those who by faith name God, behold, they have shown themselves to have received the blessing by their own mouth, so that they may be offspring of the new law of that holy land
which he promised beforehand, and may be found fellow heirs; and further, those who were neither justified by works of the law nor brought to repentance by faith,
so that they might glorify Christ, they themselves being justly condemned as guilty. For Moses also spoke beforehand, and through that teaching he shows us the type:
"And these also shall stand for the blessings: Simeon, Levi, Judah, Zebulun, Joseph, Benjamin", through whom Christ was prefigured beforehand:
he was born, and was made manifest, and we believed in him, and he was glorified, and he was recognized through Joseph, from Levi and from Judah.
As king and priest he was born in the flesh. He was recognized by Simeon in the temple, for he said:
"Now dismiss your servant in peace, Lord, for my eyes have seen your salvation, which you prepared before the face of all peoples.
A light has shone forth upon the Gentiles, and the glory of your people Israel." And through Zebulun the nations believed, as the prophet says:
"Land of Zebulun and land of Naphtali, the way of the sea, beyond the Jordan.
The people who sat in darkness saw a great light, and on those who sat in the shadows of death a great light has shone."
And Benjamin: through Paul the apostle he was preached in all the world and glorified.
And there is confirmation [?] also through those of former times, who beforehand carried this out in the figure of the law.
But now it has been fulfilled by Christ in the Spirit, and the blessings were given on Mount Gerizim,
as chosen by a new law, through which Christ, made flesh, appeared to the world and was found on the holy mountain.
As Isaiah says: "In the last times the mountain of the Lord will be made manifest."
And the curses were given on Mount Ebal, which he also spoke to those who were under the law:
"Cursed be everyone who does not abide by all the writings of the book of the law, to do it."
With all our ability, let us see what Moses says in those blessings he uttered.
For the scripture says this: These are the blessings with which Moses, the man of God, blessed the sons of Israel, and he spoke them before his death:
"The Lord came from Sinai and hastened from Mount Paran and with the myriads of Kadesh. At his right hand with him were his angels.
And he had mercy on his people, and all the holy ones are in his hands, and these are under you.

And he received from his mouth the law which Moses commanded us, a dwelling in the midst of Jacob, and by that beloved one he shall be ruler at the gathering of the people, together with the tribes of Israel."
This is what the prophet said: he shows us the help given to the people, together with the tribes of Israel, the contest waged by God against the foreigners,
against Sihon king of the Heshbonites and Og king of the Bashanites, among whom he appeared with angels to deliver them from their enemies, showing mercy to the people.
This must be understood of the coming of the Lord, for he who appeared to Moses on Mount Sinai,
he will come with angels and deliver the saints from their oppressing pursuers, by mercy on those who trust in him, for it says:
"All the sanctified are in your hands." Who could be the protector and refuge of all, except the Lord alone,
who spread out his arms and sanctified all who flee to him, like a bird that gathers its chicks?
And Ezra foretold similar things: Blessed is the Lord, who spread out his hands and saved Jerusalem.
And through Isaiah he reproaches those disobedient ones and says to them: "I have stretched out my hands all day long to a disobedient people."
And here he says to Moses: "All the sanctified are in your hands, and these are under you."
And "he received by his words the laws which Moses commanded us, the inheritance of the assembly of Jacob."
Now who received the laws from whom by those words, if not the Son from the Father?
He it is who, appearing in a cloud on Mount Sinai, gave them to Moses, he who had received the law from the Father,
for, having come down, the Son, as mediator by the commandment of the Father, lays down a testimony among that people, in this inheritance of the sons of Jacob.
The law came through Moses, and Moses was the mediator between the Son and the people through the giving of the ordinance of the law. For Jeremiah also says something like this:
"This is our God, and there is no other besides him. He found all the ways of knowledge and gave them to Jacob his servant and to Israel his beloved."
And all wisdom and learning, found by the Father, he gave to the Son, whom the prophet designates as Jacob and Israel, who is the firstborn Son of God; and the Son has received all wisdom.
He bestowed it graciously on human beings, as it says: "After this he shall appear on earth and live among human beings."
For Moses too first gave to their fathers the law which he had received from the Son.
And after this he taught their sons the law which he had received from the Son.
And after this he taught their sons a second law, in order to show the two laws:
the old one he appointed for their fathers with circumcision, and the new one he kept for the new people.
Now he who ordained the old through Moses is the same who shows us the new, for he alone is the one and only God, who was proclaimed through them, invisible [and] believed [?].
And he is the only Son of God, who appeared to the world so that it might believe, as he says through Jeremiah:
"And it shall be in those days, says the Lord, that I will lay upon the house of David and upon the house of Judah a new covenant, not such as I promised to their fathers on Mount Horeb."
Now the Son of God [?], who has been the mediator of all things between God and human beings, first through a cloud, as through a mirror,
He appeared to Moses on the mountain and gave the law as a command from the Father, as Scripture says: "And the Lord said to Moses:
'Go down and command the people: if you diligently keep the commandments of the Lord your God and do what is pleasing before him,
I will not send upon you any of the plagues that I brought upon the land of Egypt, for I am the Lord your God.'"
Now who is that Lord who spoke to Moses, if not the Son? Or whose law was he commanding, if not the Father's? He wished to reveal his own judgment and said:
"All the plagues that I brought upon the Egyptians I will not bring upon you." And he did not speak thus, as of the one who sent him:
"For the Father judges no one, but has given all judgment to the Son," who judged the Egyptians, justly drowned in the Red Sea?
Deuteronomy rightly says: "He received laws from his mouth,
which Moses commanded us, an inheritance of the people of Jacob," and "there shall be a ruler through the beloved of the Lord," so that at that time he might appear to Moses as a ruler, trustworthy.
When that beloved Son of God appears from heaven in glory together with Moses, and what was preached by him
is shown openly to all, that which he then told Moses on the mountain and no one believed.

And now he was made manifest to the world as a man among them and was not recognized [?], as Moses himself speaks of the assembly of the rulers together with the tribes of Israel. Therefore the apostles also said something like this:
"Lord, you are the one who made heaven and earth and the sea and everything, who spoke through the mouth of your beloved servant David:
'Why did the nations gather together like brute beasts, and the people plot vain things?'"
The kings of the earth conspired and the rulers gathered together against the Lord and against his anointed.
Truly, Herod and Pontius Pilate, together with the people and the authorities, gathered against your Son Jesus,
to do whatever your hand and your right hand had prepared beforehand."
And Moses began to bless them and said: "Let Reuben live and not die, and let him be many in number."
Now if anyone supposes that this was said about Reuben, he is mistaken, for Reuben had died long before and was buried in the land of Egypt.
Indeed, David also speaks beforehand about Christ in similar words: "I shall not die, but I shall live." Likewise Moses also says:
"Let Reuben live and not die, and let him be many in number." This is now being fulfilled through the churches among the nations, and the children of the barren woman are more numerous
than those of the woman who has a husband. This is a sign of the resurrection. Moses foresaw the resurrection of the Lord, that death would have no dominion over him, and he said:
"Let him live and not die." For David too could not have said this about himself:
"I shall live and not die", since he died, and his tomb lies there to this very day.
but he too foresaw the resurrection of the Lord, that death would have no power over him. He said: "Let him live and not die."
But he who also foresaw the resurrection of the Lord also prophesies to the believers, and the apostle says:
"He who died, died to sin once, but he who lives, lives to God."
And when it says, "He died through sin," it clearly teaches us that:
"For the sake of all sinful men, he to whom death was not due was given over to death for us all,
so that those who live might no longer live for themselves, but for him who died for them and rose again."
And: "If we die with Christ through baptism, we believe that he, having risen from the dead, will die no more, and death will have no dominion over him."
This was what Moses was saying: "Let him live and not die, and let him be many in number."
And of Judah too: "Hear, Lord, the voice of Judah, and gather him in to his assembly! And let his hands judge, and may he become a helper against enemies."
Now all the divine books and all the prophets strive after nothing else, but cry out concerning the Savior, so that by every means they may bring the races of men to submission.
And they do this not in vain, but because they knew that the races of men are slow to believe.
He saw their free will, for it easily tips toward what is worthless rather than toward what is better.

For this reason the Spirit labors through all the Scriptures for the manifestation of Christ, so that he may bring the hearers to submit to believing the things that have been said, through which they may be able to live, and as it says: "Lord, the voice of Judah".
It shows us that Christ was to be born in the flesh from Judah, he who entreats at all times, making prayer to the Father with mercy on behalf of the saints.
And he entrusts them to the Father. And in the Gospel it is written in the same way: "The Lord lifted up his eyes to heaven and said: 'Father, I thank you.
I know that you always hear me, and now I speak because of this multitude that surrounds me, so that they may know that you sent me.'"
And again: "Father, keep these holy in this world. I pray to you for them.
And not only for them, but also for those who are prepared to believe in your name through me."
So too Moses says: "Hear, Lord, the voice of Judah, and gather into the congregation."
Who, then, would come to his congregation, but those blessings and prayers which the Son prayed to the Father on behalf of the saints?
And as for what he said, "His hands shall judge": these are the hands that were nailed to the wood.
He will judge created beings, showing everyone at that time the mark of the nails in his hands, as John says:
"They will look on him whom they pierced." And further he says:
"Be a helper against his enemies," for the Father helped him and delivered him from enemies and plotters, as Jacob says:
"Your hands are on the backs of your enemies." And David says:
"Many dogs have surrounded me, and the assembly of the wicked has hemmed me in," for "I was cast upon you from my mother's womb.
You are the one to whom I entrust myself." The Father exalted him and seated him on the thrones of glory, to whom he says:
"Sit at my right hand, until I make your enemies a footstool for your feet." This was what Moses foretold:
"Hear, O Lord, the voice of Judah." And they will come to his assembly. And his hands will judge.
And may you be a helper against his enemies." And again concerning Levi he speaks in the same manner: "Give to Levi his manifestation
and his justice to the holy man, whom they tested with trial and whom they reproached at the waters of dispute,
who said to his father and mother, 'I do not know you,' and to his brothers, 'I do not know you.'
And he did not acknowledge his own children. He kept your words and did not transgress your covenant.
They shall make known your judgment to Jacob and your law to Israel; they shall offer incense at the time of wrath upon him and upon your offerings.
Bless, Lord, his strength, and accept the works of his hands.
He will break the strength of his enemies who rise up, and those who hate him will not rise." And as for what he said:
"Give to Levi manifestation": with these words he reveals Christ as priest of the most high and invisible God, who afterwards put on manifestation and truth;
the two laws held up on both shoulders down to the ankle [?]: manifestation is the Law, truth is the Gospel, so that he might be shown to be a perfect priest by the perfect Father.
As he says through David the prophet: "You are a priest forever after the order of Melchizedek." And Nathan says:
"The Lord will raise up for himself a faithful priest, who will do and fulfill all the will of his heart." For he was prepared.
Christ, from the tribe of Levi, from the established priesthood, from the tribe of Aaron, likewise born in the flesh, was made eternal priest by the Father.
Moses proclaimed beforehand and said: "Give to Levi his manifestation, and his justice to the holy man."
You see now how he revealed the man as a name for him. He alone has revealed justice to us, and when he said:
"His justice to the holy man," he also shows him to us as a man, the one who was to appear afterward.
As Peter, crying out openly to the rulers, said:
"Jesus of Nazareth, a man of God, made manifest among you by signs and miracles which he performed through God among you,
this one, shown forth by the counsel and knowledge of God, you handed over into the hands of the lawless and killed by nailing him to the cross; whom God raised up, having loosed the bonds of hell."
And Moses says: "Give to Levi his blessing, and his justice to the holy man."
And so that no one would think Christ a mere man, Moses spoke with care:
"Those who tested him in the testing reproached him at the waters of strife."
Now where did they test him and reproach him? In the wilderness, of course, where the people murmured against Moses and Aaron and said:
"Give us water to drink. Why did you bring us out of the land of the Egyptians to kill us and our children with thirst?"
And Moses said to them: "Why do you reproach us, and why do you test the Lord?" "This murmuring of yours is not against us, but against God."
The Lord said to Moses: "I have heard the murmuring of the sons of Israel," which they murmur against you.
"And now take with you some of the elders at dawn, and I will stand on that rock at Horeb until you come, and you shall strike that rock with the staff
with which you struck the sea, and water will come out of the rock, and the people will drink." And the name of that place was called Testing and Reproach, for they tested God, saying:
Is the Lord with us or not? Now who is it that said to Moses:
"I will stand on that rock at Horeb until you come"? Surely the one concerning whom Moses said:
Give to Levi his manifestation, and his justice to the holy man, whom they tempted in the testing, and reproached him at the waters of dispute.
If he existed beforehand, before he had yet put on flesh, he was not only a man; and if he revealed himself by word to Moses in the desert, he was not merely a man.
This one, sent and made manifest, he has shown to us as God, saying: "They drank from the spiritual rock that followed them, and that rock was Christ."
He recounts this in detail on account of those who understand wrongly, both those who diminish Christ in respect of his divine part and those who ascribe suffering to the Father of all,
who cannot look into the Scriptures with an upright mind, and who bring destitution [?] upon themselves.
And Moses says: "Who says to father or mother: I do not know you." The Lord shows this plainly in the Gospel, when certain people who stood before him said to him:
"Behold, your father and mother and brothers are standing outside and wish to see you. He said to them: Who is my mother, or who are my brothers?
But whoever does the will of my Father who is in heaven, that one is my mother and brother."
And by this plain teaching, given to us beforehand by the Savior, he makes us obedient to leave parents and brothers
who are so according to the flesh, and to follow the heavenly Father, so that we may be sons of God.
From now on we are no longer to be as fleshly people who have died, but are to serve by the Spirit of God and be found in heaven as offspring of God.
For this reason too Moses says: "He did not know his brothers and did not recognize his offspring."
He speaks of the brothers whom people supposed to be his brothers according to the flesh. These the Savior did not know, for in truth they were not brothers,
since they had been born of Joseph by seed, while he was born of the Virgin and by the Holy Spirit, and yet they supposed them to be his brothers.
But he did not know them, for it says: "And he did not know his children."
Which children, if not that race of the sons of Israel, whom he called co-heirs through the law?
A holy congregation, a race chosen above all races, shown forth as his own special possession [?].
But because they were not manifest toward him [?] he did not know them, just as he says through Isaiah: "I have begotten sons and raised them up, and they have despised me."
Now those whom they supposed to be his brothers according to the flesh, and who became known by him, and those who had been called to the inheritance,
For they had become offspring of lawlessness and an evil seed, and they were justly cast out by him. What does Moses say?
"They kept your words; they did not transgress your covenant." Who kept whose words?
None other than the only Son of the Father, who came to fulfill the law of the Father and willed to fulfill the new law by himself.
As he says: "I did not come to do my own will, but the will of my Father who sent me."
And again he says: "I do nothing of myself, but what I see my Father doing, that I do."
So then he indeed kept his commandments and did not transgress his covenant. For this reason too the Father says through the mouth of Zechariah:
"If you call upon [?] my commandments and keep my orders, you shall judge my house; you shall make known my judgments to Jacob and my law to Israel."
Who were those who made us understand justice, if not the apostles, who became disciples of the Lord?
They plainly preached the Gospel to all, first as to the people of the sons of Jacob, and then to the nations, as to their own children, to the sons of Israel.
"And let them burn perpetual incense upon your altar." What then is that altar, if not the heavenly one alone,
or what sort of incense, if not the prayers of the saints from the mouth of the saints, burned for the glory of God and offered as a sweet fragrance before God?
As Isaiah says: "They will worship you and pray to you, for God is with you, and there is no other God besides you,
for you are God, and we know no other God, savior of Israel, besides you.
Let all who rose up to attack him be turned back and put to shame." And Moses says:
"Bless, O Lord, his strength, and accept the works of his hands," for everything which the Son did.
was offered to God; he healed the sickness of human beings, so that because of this the whole world might be able to live.
"Let the strength of his enemies be crushed, and let those who hate him not rise up." He does not say this to mean:
"Let them not rise at all." Those who hate Christ and do not believe in him will not rise to judgment; see, they are already judged. As David says:
"The ungodly will not rise in the judgment, nor sinners in the council of the righteous, for the Lord knows the way of the righteous, but the way of the ungodly will perish."
Now the blessed Moses blesses Levi and passes over Simeon. It is fitting for us to show the reason
why he mentioned the eleven tribes and did not bring forward the tribe of Simeon.
The reason was this: the children of Israel made the image of a calf in the wilderness and worshiped it as a god.
And Moses, when he had come down from the mountain and saw their evil deeds, stood and cried out loudly [?] in the struggle [?] and said:
"If anyone is the Lord's, let him come to me." Then all the kindred of Levi came to him. And he said to them: "Thus says the Lord:
Let each man draw his sword and pass from gate to gate, and let each one slay his brother and each one his neighbor."
And the sons of Levi did as Moses had commanded them. And on that day about three thousand men fell. And Moses said to them:
"Now lift up your hands to the Lord to receive a blessing." And the sons of Levi carried out this judgment, and so did those of Simeon, who were brothers from one mother,
They did not hasten, nor were they zealous, as they were zealous for Dinah, their sister, who was unlawfully defiled by Shechem, the son of Hamor.
Rightly did Moses bless Levi and pass over Simeon. But if someone should say: How is it that it is written in the Law:
"You shall not kill," and "Whoever kills his brother is liable to death," and yet these men, by slaughtering their brothers, receive blessing and praise?
But it is one thing to kill a sinner and another to kill a righteous man. It is evident, for Phinehas too, the son of Eleazar,
the son of Aaron the priest, went into the chamber [?] and pierced through the harlot and Zimri, and he was not counted among murderers, but received praise and blessing from the Lord.
For when he saw them embracing one another, he pierced them through with the sword, and by his own hand he did away with the lawlessness of the people through that public display.
If this is so, when someone kills a sinner, he is not condemned along with murderers. But if someone unlawfully kills a righteous person, as a murderer,
he is condemned. For the rulers of this world too continually destroy sinners by their law and judgment, and for that killing they pay no penalty.
If someone kills lawlessly, he is a murderer, and as a murderer he shall be punished like them.
Here too we must understand that those who pursued zeal for God and slew those liable to death received blessing and praise, so that others, being frightened, would sin no more.
And concerning Simeon, because of the reason that was spoken of, it remains for us to speak about him a second time, for we find that the blessed Joseph also,
For he bound Simeon before his brothers and put him in prison for three days, concerning whom he also said:
"You shall not come out from here until your youngest brother comes."
Now what is the reason for the confinement of Simeon, and not of the others among them?
For when Joseph was sent to them at their pasturing, he counseled his brothers and said: "Come, let us kill him and see what will become of those dreams of his."
Judah commands that he be sold, but Simeon that he be killed, so that the type might be preserved and the truth concerning Christ might be revealed:
sold by Judah for thirty pieces of silver and killed by Simeon.
Those who were the scribes, who spoke [?] upon that false testimony:
for it was necessary that it be foretold by all the law and by the prophets,
so that when the truth came, all this would be made known, and what was lacking from it would be filled up by the Gospel.
The Scriptures show us more perfectly what Joseph said: "He shall not go out from here until that youngest brother of yours comes here."
Then Simeon was released from imprisonment and his brothers were blessed by Joseph, when that youngest brother of theirs, who was Christ, went down to Egypt.
Those who believe in the forgiveness of sins are forgiven, and those who had been held in the bonds and shadows of death
have been delivered from judgment, and he will send down blessing from heaven upon all; for through Simeon, Christ, recognized in the temple, was speaking prophetically:
"Now, Lord, let your servant depart in peace, according to your word." According to what word? Rather, according to that which he spoke through Joseph, namely:
"You shall not go out from here until that youngest brother of yours comes"?
If this is so, he was sent by the Father as redeemer and savior not only for the twelve tribes, but for all nations, and he did not come in such a way
as to save only one part of the nations, but all the nations, as the prophet says concerning him:
"At that time they shall say to those who were in prison: Come out, and you who are in darkness, be enlightened."
Behold, we men who in former times were confined in prison by sin,
have now been freed from our bonds by Christ, and we who in former times lived darkened in the world
now, with enlightened eye, proclaim the word of God, so that what is inconceivable among men may be made possible by God.
It was not possible for men to rise from the dead, and behold, Christ has risen from the dead, so that through him our resurrection might be made known;
it was not possible for men to ascend to heaven, and behold, Christ is king of heaven, so that through him our citizenship in the heavens might be revealed;
it was not possible for man, who begets in corruption, to live forever, and behold, this has been accomplished by Christ,
so that we might believe concerning the future holy bodies, that they will be incorruptible and live eternally.
Now what was impossible for men has been made possible by God.
And who does this but the Son, or whose will is it but the Father's, by whom men are saved?
And the one who was formerly made hateful to God has now, through obedience, been made beloved by God.
But he spoke that sharp word concerning Simeon. Let us see after this what Moses says, for the scripture says: "And to Benjamin he said:
'The beloved of the Lord shall dwell in hope, and God shall be his protector all the days, and he rested between his shoulders.'"
Now who was that beloved of the Lord but Paul the apostle, who was born of the tribe of Benjamin, was selected by the Lord as a chosen vessel, and was sent into the world as a preacher of the truth?
For it says: "He shall dwell in hope." He left the synagogue, as the apostle himself says, for "whatever gain I had from the law, I have counted as sin for the sake of Christ.
And I have counted everything as worthless [?], so that I may gain Christ and be found in him, not having any righteousness of my own that I had from the law,
but that which is through faith in Christ Jesus." Truly Moses spoke well indeed when he said: "He shall dwell in hope.
And may God be his protector all the days," for as he was setting out and going to Damascus, the Lord appeared and became his protector, and by his own power he worked miracles.
And in his name, at all times and in all cities, he performed miracles.
"He rested between his shoulders," for Paul believed in the cross of the Lord, on which he stretched out his arms.
Resting upon this, he was justified. And Isaiah says beforehand: "Whose dominion was upon his shoulders."
This is he himself, for he carried the cross on his shoulder, and at the crucifixion he stretched out both his arms, so that what was said might be fulfilled, namely:
"He rested between his shoulders." For the Apostle also says: "I have been crucified with Christ; it is not I who live, but Christ lives with me."
And as long as I am alive, I now live by faith in God and through Jesus Christ, who loved me and gave himself as a ransom for me."
And concerning Joseph he says: "By the blessing of the Lord is his land, from the seasons of heaven, and from the dew, and from the springs of the deep, and from the changes of the sun's disk,
and from the conjunctions of the months with one another, and from the summits of the mountains from the beginning, and from the fullness of the seasons.
And may the favor of him who appeared upon the bush come upon the head of Joseph and upon the crown of the one glorified among his brothers.
The beauty of a firstborn young bull is his, the horn of a unicorn, his horns. And with them he shall strike down the nations from end to end.
These are the myriads of Ephraim and these the thousands of Manasseh." And in Joseph, Christ depicted himself by the figure of his life,
Just as, ahead of those words, Moses speaks of him in succession, distributing those blessings to his race. And what he says, namely:
"Blessed of the Lord is his land" can be said of Mary, who became a blessed land, and the Word came down like dew.
It may also be said of the Church, for it was blessed by the Lord as a holy land and a paradise of delight.
It is also fitting with regard to the Savior himself, for it says, "By the blessing of the Lord is his land."
For he was born of the Virgin by the Holy Spirit; the holy land, revealed in later times, inherited all the blessings of the Lord,
which he foretells to us, those that were to come for the fathers in the land of promise. Let no one suppose this to be anything else, for God said to them:
"I will give you the land that flows with milk and honey, which I promised to give to your fathers," which foretells to us the coming forth of the Word from the bosom of the Father,
after which the Savior, born on earth, was shown to be pleasing and from the Father, for he had with him the milk, that is, the old Law.
And by the establishing of the new covenant, he calls the sweetness of the Word honey, by which the bitternesses of our souls are made sweet.
For this reason the prophet of the Psalms speaks as from the cloud:
"Blessed of the Lord is his land, from the seasons of heaven, and from the dew, and from the springs of the deep,"
so that he might show us both his birth and how he was born, and might reveal his resurrection. And because he said:

"From the seasons of heaven and from the dew," [this means] that his birth is not from seed but from the Holy Spirit; and "from the springs of the abysses," because he came up from hell and from the abysses.
And from the seasons come the plants, the changes of the sun, and the gathering together of the months, for that sun rose from the earth and the eternal day was revealed.
The twelve apostles he has shown to us as twelve hours, so that through them the day might appear, as the prophet says:
"This is the day that the Lord has made; let us rejoice and be glad in it."
And as for what he said about the gathering of the months: the twelve apostles, gathered together like the twelve months, spread abroad Christ, the perfect year.
And the prophet also says: "To proclaim the acceptable year of the Lord and the day of recompense."
And since Christ is the day, the sun, and the year, it is right to call the apostles months and hours.
Moses says: "From the tops of the mountain from of old, and from the tops of the everlasting mountains."
By the top of the mountains he means the patriarchs, for they came first. The everlasting hill is the name he gives to the prophets,
for the Word was portrayed from the beginning by the patriarchs and was spread abroad by the prophets, and at the time of fulfillment,
as the fulfiller of the Law and the prophets, it is he who speaks through the prophets, he who said:
"I am near, like the seasons upon the mountains, and the good pleasures of the one who appeared in the bush, which also rested upon the head of Joseph."
Now who is it that appeared to Moses in the bush? It is he who has now come into the world.
And in the church, as in that bramble bush, he speaks to the saints, he who rescued his people from the land of the Egyptians,
who was angered at Pharaoh and punished the Egyptians, and delivered those holy ones from their servitude.
This is he who was first prefigured in Joseph, and was glorified among the brothers and blessed by the father, concerning whom Moses says: "The firstborn of the bull, his is the beauty."
For as a holy calf, an offering offered to God, clothed with the nakedness [?] of the two laws, he took counsel [?] with that power of the Spirit.
"The horn of the unicorn: his horns." You see, here he has clearly shown us the power of the cross, for there were horns on the right and on the left,
Whose horns he made to grow like a bull's, so that he might be offered as a holy offering to the Father, and the breath of fragrance might rise up to heaven. "The horn of the unicorn — his horns."
The unicorn is the wood which they set up on the earth, which tears down the unbelieving nations by goring, but gathered the believers into his own kingdom; and he says:
"These are the myriads of Ephraim, and the thousands of Manasseh." And the thousands were those sealed from his people, while the myriads were those called from the nations.
Ephraim and Manasseh show us the figure of two laws. Joseph had two sons, as we have truly explained the words concerning them in another place.
And to Zebulun he said: "Rejoice, Zebulun, in your going out, and Issachar in their tents; the nations have fallen.
And appear [?] there, offer sacrifices of righteousness, so that the wealth of the sea may suckle you, and the merchandise of the traders who dwell on the seashore."
And concerning Zebulun, as Jacob blessed him; for Jacob says:
"Zebulun shall dwell by the seashore and be a haven for ships, and shall reach as far as Sidon."
As we have seen, this blessing is now being fulfilled for the believers through the calling of the nations.

The bay for ships and the resting place is the Lord, and the ships are the churches, which, through the trials of this world, flee for refuge to the Lord from the oppression and assaults of alien spirits, as ships take refuge in a calm harbor.
And he reached as far as Sidon through the preaching of the apostles, which reached the nations dwelling far away, as the Psalmist says:
"Their voice has gone out into all the earth, and their words to the ends of the world." Similarly Moses also says:
"Rejoice, Zebulun, in your goings out." And by "goings out" he does not mean the going out from Egypt.
For it was not only Zebulun who went out from there, but all the tribes.
But those who are now called in the Gospel stand ready to depart from this world to another world.
The prophet proclaims this beforehand in his preaching to all who trust in Christ. He says:
"Rejoice, Zebulun, in your goings out," for those who leave this world in holiness rejoice in the hope of the resurrection.
and those who rest in the bosom of the Father are glad to dwell in that incorruptible age and to enter that paradise of delight.
Solomon says: "Prepare your works for your going out, and go out to the fruits. And follow in my footsteps, and raise your houses on high."
He admonished Zebulun and Issachar in order to show the ascent of the two laws to Christ through justification. And Zebulun is translated "gift," and Issachar "labor."
And those who work the vineyard well, and whose fruit is pleasing, shall receive life, like those workers of the vineyard.
But he said: "Give them their wages, and begin from the last up to the first." "Now rejoice, Zebulun, in your goings out,
"And Issachar, in his dwellings": he means the dwellings of the cities, which are settled in the holy churches:
"And there you shall call [?], and you shall offer sacrifices of righteousness.
And whom should we call upon, if not that Lord of heaven, and what offering should we offer him, if not the prayer we send up from the mouth?
"And the wealth of the sea shall suckle you." By the wealth of the sea he means, in a spiritual understanding, the nations, who through faith suck out that heavenly Spirit as if it were milk.
And the gain of merchants — of those who dwell on the seashore. By the merchants of the seashore he means those who acquire the precious pearl through mercy.
And of Gad he says: "Blessed is he who made Gad broad; like a lion he rested, he crushed the arms of the rulers, and he saw my dominion,
For there the land of the rulers who were gathered together was divided, along with the authority of the princes.
He carried out the justice of the Lord and judgment in Israel." And about what he said:
"The man who enlarges": for the blessing of the Lord spread over the breadth of the earth to the nations. And about what he said:
"Like a lion he rested," it is like those words of Jacob, who said concerning Judah:
"You crouched [?] and slept like a lion and like a whelp," so as to reveal his rest upon the earth.
And as for what he said: "They crushed the arms of the rulers," he speaks of those rulers who cried out against him, and of him
who by the rest of death crushed the arms of the devil, his principalities and powers being trampled down.
"And he saw his dominion, for there was scattered also the land of the rulers of the peoples."
By that beginning of his he means the saints, who are of the earth, of the dust, and have risen from the dead.
For Jesus became the firstborn of the dead and the beginning of all. And as for what he said:
"There the land of those assembled rulers was divided, with the nations and with the princes of the peoples," he foretells to us all those gathered to him from the four ends of the earth,
who, gathered by him from all nations and peoples, share out that holy land by reigning with Christ.
And as for what he said: "He did the justice of the Lord and his judgment in Israel,"
it is because he alone was found righteous above all men and fulfilled the will of his Father by declaring justice to that people.
For Isaiah also says: "His loins shall be girded with righteousness and his sides made firm with truth."
And to Dan he said: "Dan is a lion's whelp, and he shall begin to run from Bashan."
For Scripture calls Christ a lion and a lion's whelp because of his kingship and his power and his glory.
Moses also speaks in similar terms of the Antichrist, for that deceiver intends to imitate the Son of God in everything, and that foolish people will think that he is the Christ.
But from the holy books that foretold these things, his wickedness is known: he is the Antichrist. Jacob says:
"Dan shall be like a serpent lying in wait on the roads." And Moses says: "Dan is a lion's whelp; he shall reign for a time." And Jeremiah says:
"The sound of the swiftness of his horses shall be heard from Dan, and the whole earth shall be shaken by the sound of the neighing and of the driving [?] of his chariots."
And as for what Moses said: "He shall leap out of Bashan": for at his own time he shall suddenly appear from among the nations of bestiality and unbelief.
As Isaiah says: "They shall rush forth like lions and lions' whelps, and he shall seize [his prey] and roar.
At that time the mountains shall be enraged at his rage." He says this of his fierceness and tyranny in the struggle of war.
For this reason the prophet says: "The Lord shall turn back from Bashan to the depths of the sea, so that his foot may be dipped in blood."
And at the coming of that deceiving ruler, the Lord will appear from heaven to crush and bring down all the powers of that adversary, as Paul says:
"whom the Lord will consume with the spirit of his mouth and by the manifestation of his coming, the one whose coming will be by the power of the devil."
And to Naphtali he said: "Naphtali shall prepare the food of favour, and they shall be filled with the blessing of the Lord God, by the sea and toward the south." And concerning Naphtali he said:
"A shoot has sprung up; it has put forth its beauty from its roots." He says this to show what the saints are like: shoots in the middle of a vineyard, gladdened by good works.
But Moses says: "Naphtali, nurturer with favor," for the Lord is full of gift and grace,
so that through these things the saints may be established as a perfect man and in the measure of stature, so that they may be found perfect by the blessing from the Lord.
And because "he shall inherit toward the south," by this he secretly foretells to us the churches, which are prepared for all the world and for all creatures to inherit.
And to Asher he said: "Blessed among sons is Asher, and may he be welcoming to his brothers.
His feet shall be dipped in oil. And his shoes are of iron and bronze. And his strength is like his days.
And there is no god like the God of the Beloved, who ascends to heaven as your helper, and his establishment is in that great Sovereign and in the hidden power of God,
"And by the strength of those everlasting arms they shall drive the enemies out from before your face." And he shall say to him:
"Perish!" And Israel shall dwell in hope in that land of Jacob, among wheat and wine, and his heavens shall drip dew from the clouds.
And he speaks of the holiness of the sons of Asher, who for the sake of the name of Christ are called begotten of God, as the Evangelist says:
"To those who received that authority, he gave authority to become begotten of God, to those who believe in his name."
And John says: "God is able even from stones to raise up children to Abraham."
And Isaiah says: "Then he shall say: 'Behold, I and the children whom God has given me.'"
This the prophet Moses foretells to us by the Spirit concerning the Son who was prepared, who was to be born in the world from God, for he said:
"Blessed among brothers is Asher." And Asher is interpreted as riches, as was said before:
"The wealth of the sea shall nurse you." This wealth is the nations, who draw nourishment from the commandments of the Lord. That is why he says:
"He shall be accepted among his brothers." Are these not the ones to whom the Saviour also said, "My brothers and fellow heirs"?
By these the Word was accepted, as a man who had appeared in the flesh on earth. He was also confessed as God by them, for Thomas says:
"My Lord and my God." But his brothers according to the flesh, the very ones by whom he was known, despised him and insulted him as a poor and contemptible man.
Concerning this the prophet cries out beforehand and says: "I have begotten children and raised them up, and they have despised me.
The ox knew its owner and the donkey the manger of its lord, but Israel did not know me, and my people did not understand me."
And John bears witness to these sayings and says: "And neither did his brothers believe in him."
Now to which brothers did he become acceptable? Rather, to the distant nations who were called, to whom he also said:
"Come to me, all you who are weary and heavy-laden, and I will give you rest. Take my yoke, for I am holy and lowly in heart.
And you will receive rest for yourselves, for my yoke is sweet and my burden light?"
So that you may understand what Moses was speaking about, he says, linking it on: "Let him dip his feet in oil." Concerning the force of what was said, namely:
"He shall dip his foot in oil" means nothing other than his sufferings, for the blood that poured from his side was proclaimed to us as mercy.
The Lord's foot was dipped so that the purple-coloured mark on it might appear, fulfilled at that time, and so that the door of life might be taught to us.
And the blood of the lamb was smeared on the two doorposts of those who believed, and the destroyer fled because of it.
"Let him dip his foot in oil." This is he himself by whom mercy was done to all people; he proclaimed it beforehand, for Jacob says likewise:
"He washed his adornment in wine and his garment in the blood of grapes," in order to show that flesh clothed with that blood,
as the adornment of the Word, who also came to those sufferings, who was the Word that cannot suffer and cannot be scourged.
"Iron and bronze are his sandals." And he says this of the power of the Gospel, or else he speaks of the apostles, who became strong as iron,
enduring everything with courage, and fair-sounding as bronze through the spreading abroad of the Gospel of Christ, as the prophet says:
"How beautiful are the feet of those who bring good news of peace, who bring good tidings."
The apostles became the feet of Christ, and the Gospel their sandal. And as for what he said:
"And like your days is your strength," for he was not subject to the count of times, so as to become corruptible, but was eternal, so as to give life even to the dead.
There is no other God, more than that Beloved. After God, who else is reckoned God?
This is the Father of the beloved Son, as he testifies in the Gospel:
"A voice came from heaven and said, 'This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased. Listen to him.'" Moses also said something like this:
"There is no God like the beloved one, who sits in the heavens as your helper." And Jacob, blessing Joseph, said this to him:
"And my God helped you." And David says: "My helper and my deliverer and my glory and the one who lifts up my head."
Now he who sits in the heavens became his helper, and ours too, who trust in him, with very great assurance, for the Son,
exalted to heaven, became exalted and glorious, a glorifier and honored, established in glory upon the thrones of the Father.
As the prophet says: "His strength covered the heavens," and David says:
"Glory and wealth and might you have put upon him." And again he says: "Gird your sword upon your loins, O mighty one; array yourself, go forth prosperously, and reign!"
And Moses says: "And the covering of the divinity of that dominion, and from the mighty ones of the everlasting arms."
By "the covering of the divinity" he meant that flesh in which the Word was covered; the word indicates to us the dominion of God.
Solomon says: "The Lord created me at the beginning of the ways of his works." And John says: "I am the beginning and I am the end."
Now that flesh was the covering of the Word, who "was from the beginning with God."
The Son of God and Word of the Father loved that holy flesh, and the Father guards the Son in his arms, which have become his protector,
So that he might show him forth as eternal King and subject his enemies and the deceitful beneath him. As the prophet says:
"The Lord said to my Lord: 'Sit at my right hand, until I make your enemies a footstool under your feet.'"
And the apostle says: "He has subjected all things beneath his feet. The last enemy shall be abolished: death."
And Moses likewise says: "He shall drive out the enemy from before you and say: Perish!
And Israel shall dwell in hope in that land of Jacob, amid wheat and wine, and the heavens above you with cloud mingled with dew."

After the fall of the devil and of all his peoples, together with the destruction and abolition of their lawless deeds from the earth, "Israel shall dwell, each one apart, in hope in that land of Jacob."
At that time all the saints will reign with Christ.
Israelites are called those who see God, dwelling forever in the holy land in hope, no longer afraid of death,
nor any longer terrified by that eternal fire, nor bound by the desire of this world, nor made merry by corruptible food,
nor left empty by care for this land, nor weighed down by scorching heat or by the frosts of winter,
nor eating this food of the earth with care and sweat, for sins have been silenced, desires have been stilled, death has been conquered,
the deceiver has been trampled down, that tyrant has been wiped out, that treacherous serpent has been killed, created beings have been set free, every tree of the wilderness has been made glad.
The earth, full of fruit, stands incorruptible forever, no longer corrupted by the changing of the seasons, nor longing for rain and dew.
For these created beings have been freed from the slavery of corruption, together with the angels and human nature and all fruitfulness,
in which they offer praise to God, brought to life by the Holy Spirit,
and made fruitful by him through blessing, from which the saints taste that incorruptible bread of life.

And the spiritual angels drink the incorruptible cup through the Word, the Son. Established in unceasing hymnody, together with all creation they make their offering to God, whose glory is forever and ever. Amen.
